overview: Colonial Louisiana connected Gulf settlements with the Mississippi valley through French claims, trade and settlement. Indigenous peoples, Africans and Europeans shaped its life under deeply unequal conditions. This map shows a limited Gulf-area slice; neither its outline nor its 1715 to 1783 dates represents the entire colonial territory or history.

periods.title: French colonial Louisiana
periods.summary: French settlement developed around Gulf ports and the Mississippi; New Orleans was founded in 1718.

periods.title: Partition and Spanish administration
periods.summary: France ceded territory to Spain and Britain; New Orleans and the western portion came under Spain before retrocession to France.

periods.title: Transfer to the United States
periods.summary: The Louisiana Purchase began another change of government, with local transfers occurring after the treaty.

items.text: Excavations at Old Mobile, capital of French Louisiana from 1702 to 1711, have uncovered the sites of eight buildings and thousands of objects. These remains preserve an early phase before the map’s start, showing a colony made of particular settlements rather than continuous occupation across its vast claims.

At Port Dauphin, the port serving French Mobile from 1702 to about 1725, archaeologists uncovered houses and a barrel well. A container made for storing goods could become part of a water-supply structure. Ordinary construction details help explain how a settlement functioned.

Indigenous people taught settlers ways to prepare maize and supplied powdered sassafras, or filé, to thicken stews. Corn could be boiled, roasted or ground; treating kernels with lye produced hominy. Local knowledge helped newcomers turn unfamiliar ingredients into everyday meals.

In 1718, colonial administrators sought rice from West Africa together with enslaved people knowledgeable about its cultivation. African expertise helped shape Louisiana’s food history, but it arrived through a system that forced people to labor far from their homes.

New Orleans was founded in 1718 beside a bend of the Mississippi. Engineers laid out a regular street grid despite the surrounding swamps and risk of flooding. The plan survives in the French Quarter, a lasting trace of an ambitious and difficult urban project.

After fires in 1788 and 1794, Creole townhouses became common in rebuilt New Orleans. Their courtyards contained service spaces, and toilets were typically separate privies at the rear. A handsome street-facing house could still require a trip outdoors for the bathroom.

Twelve Ursuline nuns arrived in 1727 to establish a convent, care for the sick and educate girls. After the Natchez attack of 1729, they cared for widows and orphans of French soldiers. Their institution brought schooling and hospital work together.

The Ursulines also enslaved African and Indigenous people who cooked, cleaned and worked in the hospital. White pupils received a broad education, while enslaved residents received religious instruction only. Care and learning existed within, and helped sustain, the colony’s unequal social order.

French Louisiana repeatedly lacked enough coins. Scarcity of reliable small money complicated wages and purchases even when merchants had goods to sell. The Historic New Orleans Collection traces these problems through surviving monetary objects and administrative history.

Banque Royale notes issued in France in 1719 to 1720 helped fuel speculative excitement about Louisiana. The museum preserves a hundred-livre note dated August 1719 and a fifty-livre note from September 1720. Promises printed on paper were tied to investors’ distant hopes for colonial wealth.

“Les enfants qui naîtront de mariages entre esclaves seront esclaves” means “Children born from marriages between enslaved people will be enslaved.” This French sentence opens Article 9 of Louisiana’s 1724 Code Noir, in a published transcription. The law deliberately made enslavement hereditary.

France’s 1803 sale transferred its Louisiana claim to the United States after decades of Spanish administration. The transaction changed imperial control; it did not mean that Indigenous nations had freely sold their homelands. Colonial boundaries and the rights of people living within them were different matters.

ending.text: French rule gave way through the 1762 to 1763 partition and Spanish administration; the western territory and New Orleans passed to the United States through the 1803 purchase and subsequent transfers. Communities continued under new governments. The imported 1783 endpoint is not a single end date for colonial Louisiana.
